## /plan SKILL Output section stale: claims /plan populates the roadmap, contradicting /roadmap populate ownership

## Summary

`skills/plan/SKILL.md`'s Output section for multi-pr / roadmap input is stale: it still says `/plan` writes the roadmap's reserved Implementation Issues + Dependency Graph sections, contradicting the same skill's own ownership statement and `phase-7-creation.md`, which hand roadmap population to `/roadmap populate`.

## Evidence

- `skills/plan/SKILL.md:357-359`: "For roadmap input, populating the roadmap's reserved Implementation Issues and Dependency Graph sections is owned by `/roadmap populate` (which calls the `shirabe roadmap populate` subcommand), **not by this workflow**."
- `skills/plan/SKILL.md:~458` (Output → multi-pr mode, roadmap input): still lists "written into the roadmap's reserved sections (no separate PLAN doc)" as a `/plan` output.
- `skills/plan/references/phases/phase-7-creation.md:5-17`: "When the input is a roadmap, **do not** re-drive this phase to fill the roadmap's reserved sections by prose substitution -- that path is **retired**. ... It no longer rewrites the roadmap document itself."

## Fix

Update the `/plan` Output section (multi-pr, roadmap input) to state that roadmap population is owned by `/roadmap populate` / `shirabe roadmap populate`, and that `/plan` on a roadmap only produces a PLAN doc for a roadmap-scoped slice (per phase-7-creation.md), so the Output section stops claiming an action the workflow no longer performs.

## fix(release): require user confirmation of notes and version before draft

Restructure the /release skill's Phase 3 so the agent prints release
notes in chat and uses AskUserQuestion to confirm the version before
creating the draft release. If the user picks a different version
(e.g., patch instead of minor), the notes title is updated to match.

The draft is only created after the user approves both the notes
and the version.

---

Previously the agent went straight from note generation to
gh release create without showing the notes or confirming the version.

## fix(release): handle missing CI status on squash-merge commits

Add a fallback chain to the /release skill's CI check. Squash-merge
repos run CI on the PR branch commit, not the merge result on main. The
commit status API returns "pending" with zero check runs for these merge
commits, blocking releases unnecessarily.

The skill now tries commit status first, then falls back to the latest
workflow run on the branch if no status data exists.

---

Found during the first real release attempt (issue #38). The agent
correctly stopped at Phase 2 but the check was too strict for
squash-merge repos.

Ref #38

## fix(explore): auto-invoke downstream skills in Phase 5 handoff

Add explicit skill invocations to phase-5-produce-design.md and
phase-5-produce-prd.md so the agent loads the downstream skill after
writing handoff artifacts. Previously, these files instructed the agent
to "continue at Phase N" but never loaded the skill, leaving the agent
with no way to follow through. The fix matches the existing pattern in
phase-5-produce-decision.md, which already auto-invokes /shirabe:decision.

The routing stub (phase-5-produce.md) now documents which artifact types
auto-continue into a downstream skill and which stop execution.

---

Fixes #22

## What this accomplishes

When explore crystallizes to "design doc" or "PRD" and the user confirms,
the workflow now continues directly into /design or /prd instead of stopping
and telling the user to run a separate command.

## docs(skills): rewrite shirabe's skill descriptions to select

A skill's `description` is the only text an agent reads when deciding whether to
load a skill nobody told it to use. Most of shirabe's descriptions were spending
that budget summarizing the skill instead: pipeline coordinates that only parse
for a reader who already knows the chain, phase counts and jury sizes, state
projections and security surfaces, and trigger phrases that name the skill to an
agent who would only be reading them because nobody named it.

This rewrites sixteen of them to select. Each now leads with the job in terms an
agent can match against its own situation, fires on phrasings where nobody says
the word, says what goes wrong if it does not load, and closes by naming the
sibling skills it is genuinely confused with rather than ones nobody mixes it up
with.

Three of the changes fix wrong answers rather than wasted words. `/scope`'s
description already claimed `/design`'s and `/plan`'s requests and neither
conceded, so two skills competed for one request with only one side backing off;
both now name `/scope`, and `/design` states the niche it keeps, which is a
design when the requirements are already settled. `/prd` offered "define scope
for Y", colliding head-on with `/scope`, and now fences against `/scope` and
`/brief` instead. `/work-on` still advertised that it drives a whole plan
through one shared branch and PR, which its own body says it stopped doing when
`/execute` took over plan-level execution; both skills now state the `multi-pr`
carve-out from their own side so the two agree.

shirabe's own docs move with them. CLAUDE.md's two lists of invented trigger
phrases are gone, replaced by the situations that should reach each entry point,
and the four cold-start prompts that quoted those lists verbatim now say the same
thing in the same terms. That also closes an inconsistency live on main, where
`/scope`'s frontmatter had already dropped the phrases while its body still named
them.

---

## What changed

Sixteen `description:` fields, in four groups:

- **Tactical chain** -- `/brief`, `/prd`, `/design`, `/plan`, `/review-plan`
- **Implementation chain** -- `/work-on`, `/execute`
- **Strategic chain** -- `/charter`, `/vision`, `/strategy`, `/roadmap`
- **Standalone** -- `/comp`, `/decision`, `/explore`, `/release`, `/writing-style`

Plus `CLAUDE.md`, `README.md`, and the four files that quoted CLAUDE.md's trigger
phrases: `skills/scope/SKILL.md`,
`skills/scope/references/phases/phase-0-setup.md`, `skills/charter/SKILL.md`, and
`skills/charter/references/phases/phase-0-setup.md`.

`skills/explore/SKILL.md`'s Routing Guide moved too. It is the repo's third
selection surface -- the most complete situation-to-skill map anywhere in shirabe
-- and two of its rows contradicted the rewrites outright. "It accepts a PLAN
path and nothing else" left out both the `multi-pr` carve-out and resume, and
"This is simple, just do it" pointed at `/work-on` for work that may have no
requirements written down, which is the boundary `/work-on` now draws against
`/scope`. Both rows are corrected, along with the two Quick Decision Table rows
carrying the same two claims. The tables were edited after the descriptions were
settled, so they agree with text that exists rather than text that was planned.

`/scope`'s own `description:` field is deliberately untouched. It was rewritten
against this standard already and is the reference the other sixteen were written
to match. Only its body line naming the three CLAUDE.md phrases changed.

## Reviewed and deliberately left unchanged

Five skills were reviewed and not touched, for reasons that are about behaviour
rather than taste:

- `skills/inflight`, `skills/private-content`, `skills/public-content` carry
  `disable-model-invocation: true`. A skill with that flag never enters the
  model's available-skills listing, so its description does no selection work at
  all. Rewriting them changes nothing an agent can observe.
- The two `preflight-liveness` fixtures under `skills/inflight/evals/fixtures/`
  are deliberately anti-selection -- both open with "Eval fixture" and close with
  "Not a workflow skill and not shipped in the shirabe plugin". Rewriting them for
  selection would break exactly what they test.

## The two PRDs are not retro-edited

`docs/prds/PRD-shirabe-scope-skill.md` and `docs/prds/PRD-shirabe-charter-skill.md`
still state the removed trigger phrases, as numbered requirements. They are
durable audit-trail artifacts recording what was required at the time, and
retro-editing them would falsify that record. `git grep` for the five removed
phrases returns hits only in those two files. The same reasoning covers the one
line in `docs/designs/current/DESIGN-shirabe-progression-authoring.md` that refers
to those requirements without quoting them.

## Verification

```
bash scripts/check-skill-injection.sh     # OK (22 SKILL.md scanned, 23 injected lines)
bash scripts/check-evals-exist.sh         # All skills have evals
bash scripts/check-skill-requires_test.sh # 36 passed, 0 failed
```

Every rewritten frontmatter was parsed with a YAML loader to confirm it still
loads and the `description` value is a non-empty string. Descriptions run 801 to
1020 characters, inside the 600-1100 the existing corpus already used; no gate in
this repo enforces a ceiling.

Every row of `/explore`'s three routing tables was checked against every
rewritten negative boundary. No row now points somewhere a description says not
to go, and no row asserts something a description denies. The two tables also
deliberately route to no chain hop at all, which is what `/design` and `/plan`
conceding to `/scope` amounts to on the routing side.

## On the eval obligation

CLAUDE.md says evals must be created or updated whenever a skill is updated, and
says outright not to treat the CI existence check as a substitute for running
them. A description edit is a SKILL.md edit, so that obligation is live here and
this PR is deliberately not satisfying it with `check-evals-exist.sh` alone.

The reason is that the existing evals cannot answer the question this change
raises. Their scenarios invoke each skill explicitly -- `"prompt": "/design
authentication-system"` is representative -- so they grade what a skill does
after it has loaded. Nothing in them depends on the description text, so a
frontmatter-only change cannot move them in either direction, and a flat result
would be no evidence that the rewrite worked. Running eighteen skills' evals
would spend real model budget confirming that unrelated behaviour is unchanged.

inputs.issue_context:
## orchestrator re-spawns manually-initialized child workflows that are already complete

## Description

When a child workflow is manually initialized (via `koto init`) with a name matching one of an orchestrator's batch children, the orchestrator's batch system does not recognize it as the same workflow. The batch still shows the child as `pending`. On the next call to `koto next <orchestrator>`, the scheduler treats the child as un-spawned and materializes a new instance from `entry` state, discarding the completed work.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Start an orchestrator workflow that defines batch children (e.g., `child-a`, `child-b`).
2. Manually initialize and drive one of those children to completion: `koto init child-a && koto next child-a` (repeat until done).
3. Call `koto next <orchestrator>`.
4. Observe that the orchestrator spawns a fresh instance of `child-a` from `entry` state, ignoring the completed run.

## Root Cause

`materialize_children` does not check whether a workflow with the matching name already exists before spawning. Only workflows spawned by the orchestrator itself are registered in the batch system. A manually-initialized workflow with the same name is invisible to the batch tracker, so it is never adopted as the canonical child.

## Impact

All workflow state from the manually-initialized run is silently discarded. The completed work is lost from koto's perspective and the agent must re-drive through all states a second time. There is no warning or error — the re-spawn happens transparently.

## Observed Version

koto 0.8.1

## Workaround

- **Drive again**: Re-drive the child through the workflow a second time, submitting evidence that the work is already done.
- **Avoid manual init**: Always drive child workflows exclusively through the orchestrator. Never initialize them manually while an orchestrator is active for the same names.

## Possible Fixes

- **Option A** (adopt): `materialize_children` checks for an existing workflow with the matching name and adopts it rather than spawning a new instance. If the existing workflow is already complete, the batch child is marked done immediately.
- **Option B** (document): Document clearly that manually-initialized children of orchestrator workflows must be completed *before* the orchestrator is started, or avoided entirely while an orchestrator is active.
- **Option C** (register command): Provide a `koto batch register <orchestrator> <child-name>` command to manually register an existing workflow as a batch child, giving operators an escape hatch without requiring code changes.

Option A seems most user-friendly since it prevents silent data loss. Option C is a lower-risk complement that could be shipped independently.

## fix(work-on): keep the tests_passing gate's output readable

Keep the `tests_passing` gate's output where an operator can read it. The gate
ended in `2>/dev/null`; it now writes both streams to a file in the run's own
directory, which is what makes a run that was killed mid-command legible instead
of arriving as a bare exit code.

This is the first half of #376. The second half — whether a shared template should
run a repository's whole test suite unbounded at a state transition at all — is a
decision, and it ships separately so that a command-string repair is not held
behind a policy question.

Refs #376

---

## Why removing the redirect was not enough

koto keeps a command gate's stderr only for a spawn or wait failure. A non-zero
exit is reported as `{"exit_code": N, "error": ""}` and a timeout as
`{"error": "timed_out"}` with nothing else (`koto/src/gate.rs:281-306`). An
unredirected command would have satisfied the letter of "stop discarding stderr"
and still left an operator with an exit code and no text.

So the gate writes to `{{SESSION_DIR}}/tests_passing.log` instead. Three
properties matter and each was measured rather than assumed:

- **The verdict is unchanged.** `> file 2>&1` keeps the exit status of `go test`
  itself, which is what the transition routes on. A pipe to `tee` would report
  tee's status.
- **`{{SESSION_DIR}}` resolves inside a gate command.** It is documented as a
  reserved runtime name in a passage about directives, which an agent expands in
  its own shell; a gate is run by koto, so this was probed directly.
- **A killed command still leaves its output.** This is the case that motivated
  the issue: a run whose suite fork bombed was recorded as `timed_out` with exit
  -1 while the command had been writing evidence the whole time.

On a child session the directory is disposed of with the session, so the log
outlives the run only for a root — the same retention rule the run's record
already follows.

## The test, and the mistake in its first draft

`tests-passing-gate_test.sh` runs the expression **extracted from the template**
with `go` stubbed, so a copy pasted into the test cannot keep passing after
someone edits the real gate. Five cases: a failing suite keeps its status and its
detail reaches the log; a passing suite passes; a command killed mid-run leaves
its partial output; the replaced form is shown discarding that detail; and a
repository with no `go.mod` runs nothing at all.

Against the form it replaces, three of the five fail.

The first draft of that proof was itself wrong, in the way this family of defect
usually is. The extractor understood only the single-quoted YAML form, so against
the double-quoted form it replaced it passed the quotes through to `sh -c` and
produced a 127 "not found". The cases failed — for a reason with nothing to do
with the defect, which would have been read as proof. The extractor now handles
both quote styles, and the failures that remain are about missing output.

## What this does not change

The gate still runs `go test ./...`, still unbounded in what it may spawn, still
only in repositories that have a root `go.mod`. Whether it should is #376's
second half and is not settled here.

## run-cascade.sh: delete_plan never enters STAGED_FILES, so a PLAN-only chain never commits its own deletion

`skills/execute/scripts/run-cascade.sh` appends every artifact it transitions to `STAGED_FILES` — the ROADMAP at `:497` and `:577`, the DESIGN at `:795`, the PRD at `:802`, the BRIEF at `:808`. The PLAN deletion at `:873-879` runs `git rm -f` and records its step, but never appends.

Both the commit and the post-cascade verification are gated on that array being non-empty:

```bash
if [[ "$PUSH" == "true" ]] && [[ ${#STAGED_FILES[@]} -gt 0 ]]; then
```

So a chain whose only action is the PLAN deletion — a PLAN with no resolvable upstream — stages the deletion and then never commits it, even under `--push`.

## Reproduction

A PLAN with no `upstream:` field, cascaded with `--push`:

```
{ "cascade_status": "skipped", "steps": [lifecycle_pre_probe ok, delete_plan ok] }
CASCADE RC=0
=== git status ===  D  docs/plans/PLAN-no-upstream.md
=== git log ===     (no cascade commit)
```

The deletion is staged and left uncommitted. The run reports `skipped`, which is accurate about the chain walk — `finalize-chain` returned a one-node report — but says nothing about the uncommitted deletion.

## Why it is filed separately

Found while scoping the post-verify seed fix (PR #345). That change needed `STAGED_FILES` to be the record of what survived, and this is a gap in what the record contains rather than in how it is read, so folding it in would have widened a defect fix into two.

It also bounds what a test fixture can look like: a no-anchor `--push` scenario cannot be built on a no-upstream PLAN, because that shape exercises neither the commit nor the verification. PR #345's no-survivor scenario uses a deleted ROADMAP instead.

## Fix shape

Append `$PLAN_DOC` to `STAGED_FILES` on the successful `git rm` branch at `:874`. The path is deleted rather than surviving, so the post-verification's existence test already skips it — that test was written knowing the record can hold deleted paths, because the ROADMAP deletion at `:577` puts one there today.

Refs #345

## /scope's hop gates resolve hop-complete.sh against the wrong directory, so every gate exits 127 outside shirabe

## What happens

Every command gate in `/scope`'s koto template names `hop-complete.sh` by a path
relative to the working directory. koto runs a gate command with the working
directory of the `koto next` process, which for `/scope` is the repository being
scoped -- not the shirabe checkout. `skills/scope/scripts/` does not exist there,
so the shell exits 127 and the gate fails.

The first hop is where it lands. Driving a run in a scratch repository against
koto 0.12.2 and the shipped template:

```
== tick 4 state=hop_brief
   wants: detail outcome
{"action":"evidence_required","advanced":false,
 "blocking_conditions":[{"name":"brief_complete",
                         "output":{"error":"","exit_code":127},
                         "status":"failed","type":"command"}],
 ...}
```

`advanced` stays `false` for every subsequent tick. The run holds at `hop_brief`
and there is no way past it: submitting `landed` is refused by a gate that cannot
run, and no artifact has been written yet.

Note `"error":""`. koto reports a failed command gate as an exit status and
discards the command's own output -- `/scope`'s own directive text says so
("koto reports a failed command gate as an exit code with no message"). So the
operator sees a hop that will not advance, an exit code of 127, and nothing
naming the missing file.

It was found by running `/scope` against another repository and worked around by
symlinking shirabe's `skills/` directory into that repository's root. That is
enough to finish one run; it is not a fix.

## Where

Eight lines in `skills/scope/koto-templates/scope.md`, fourteen invocations --
the two full-run exit gates chain all four hops in one command:

```
$ grep -n "command: 'skills/" skills/scope/koto-templates/scope.md
171:  command: 'skills/scope/scripts/hop-complete.sh --hop brief  --topic "{{TOPIC}}"'
200:  command: 'skills/scope/scripts/hop-complete.sh --hop prd    --topic "{{TOPIC}}"'
234:  command: 'skills/scope/scripts/hop-complete.sh --hop design --topic "{{TOPIC}}"'
263:  command: 'skills/scope/scripts/hop-complete.sh --hop plan   --topic "{{TOPIC}}"'
295:  command: 'skills/scope/scripts/hop-complete.sh --hop plan   --topic "{{TOPIC}}"'
298:  command: 'skills/scope/scripts/hop-complete.sh --hop design --topic "{{TOPIC}}"'
446:  command: '... brief && ... prd && ... design && ... plan'   # exit_full_run
490:  command: '... brief && ... prd && ... design && ... plan'   # full_run_blocked
```

`hop-complete.sh`'s own `--root` argument is not the problem and does not want
changing: it defaults to `.`, and the working directory genuinely is the
repository root whose `docs/` tree the predicate reads. Only the path to the
script itself is wrong.

## The fix already exists in this repository

`skills/execute/koto-templates/execute.md` solved this for `settled_branch_record`
by declaring a `PLUGIN_ROOT` template variable:

```yaml
command: '{{PLUGIN_ROOT}}/skills/execute/scripts/record-settled-branch.sh "execute-{{PLAN_SLUG}}"'
```

`/execute`'s SKILL.md passes `--var PLUGIN_ROOT=${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` at
`koto init`, where the agent's own shell expands it exactly once. It has to be a
`{{KEY}}`: koto does not resolve shell variables in a field it hands to `sh -c`,
and `scripts/check-template-interpolation.sh` fails the build on a `$NAME` there
for that reason. Matching it also buys `/scope` the compile-time checking
`{{KEY}}` references get, so a later typo becomes a template error rather than an
empty expansion that silently tests the wrong path.

## What done looks like

- No command field in `scope.md` resolves a script relative to the working
  directory.
- `PLUGIN_ROOT` declared in the template's `variables:` block and supplied at
  `koto init` wherever `/scope`'s written procedure documents that call.
- The gates demonstrated resolving from a working directory that is not the
  shirabe checkout, not asserted to.

## /release drops same-day merges from the release notes

## What happens

`/release` Phase 3 step 2 gathers the PRs for the release notes with:

```
gh pr list --state merged --base main --search "merged:>$LAST_TAG_DATE"
```

`$LAST_TAG_DATE` is used but never defined anywhere in the skill. If it is
derived as a date — the reading the name invites — GitHub's search treats
`merged:>YYYY-MM-DD` as "after the end of that day", so every PR merged on the
same calendar day as the previous tag is dropped from the release notes.

Silently. The notes render as a complete list either way.

## Reproduction

Cutting v0.18.0 from v0.17.0, which was tagged `2026-08-15T19:43:30+00:00`:

```
$ gh pr list --state merged --base main --search "merged:>2026-08-15" \
    --json number --jq '[.[].number]|sort'
[292,311,316,318]

$ gh pr list --state merged --base main --search "merged:>2026-08-15T19:43:30Z" \
    --json number --jq '[.[].number]|sort'
[292,297,311,316,318]
```

#297 (`feat(validate): report and prevent references a lifecycle move
invalidates`) merged at `2026-08-15T23:52:38Z` — four hours *after* the tag, and
squarely in the release. The date-truncated form loses it.

That PR is the one that shipped `FC20` at error level. It is the single change
in v0.18.0 most likely to break an adopter's build on upgrade, so it is also the
one most costly to omit from the notes.

## Why it is easy to miss

Phase 3 step 1 already gathers `git log $LAST_TAG..HEAD`, which is exact. Step 2
then re-derives the same set through a different mechanism with different
boundary semantics. Nothing cross-checks the two, so a disagreement between them
surfaces only if the author happens to compare counts by hand.

## Suggested fix

Either would close it:

1. **Derive the PR list from the commit range** already gathered in step 1 —
   parse the `(#N)` suffixes that squash-merge writes into subjects. One source,
   no boundary semantics to get wrong, and it cannot disagree with the commits
   the release actually contains.
2. **Define `$LAST_TAG_DATE` as a full ISO-8601 timestamp** and say so, e.g.
   `LAST_TAG_DATE=$(git log -1 --format=%cI "$LAST_TAG")`. Keeps the current
   shape; relies on every future reader preserving the precision.

The first is preferable because it removes the second source rather than
tightening it, and the skill is already computing what it needs one step
earlier.

## Found during

Cutting v0.18.0. Caught by comparing the search result against
`git log v0.17.0..origin/main`; the notes shipped complete because #297 was
pulled in by number after the mismatch showed up.

## main is not cargo fmt --check clean and nothing gates formatting, so cargo fmt --all sweeps unrelated files into PRs

`main` is not `cargo fmt --check` clean, and no workflow gates on formatting.
The combination is worse than either alone: a routine `cargo fmt --all`
reformats files the author never touched, and nothing stops the result from
merging.

## Evidence

Before #283, eight files under `crates/shirabe-validate/src/` differed from
rustfmt's output: `features.rs`, `finalize.rs`, `formats.rs`, `lifecycle.rs`,
`mermaid.rs`, `pr_body.rs`, `prose.rs`, `rules.rs`.

No workflow runs `cargo fmt --check` or `cargo clippy` — `build-and-test.yml`
runs `cargo build --release` and `cargo test --workspace` and nothing else. So
the drift has no way of being noticed and no way of being corrected except by
someone running `cargo fmt` and sweeping it into an unrelated PR.

Which is what happened. #283 touched three files in that crate, ran
`cargo fmt --all`, and picked up ~350 lines of reformatting in eight files it
had no business changing. That was caught in review and reverted — and then
re-applied by a later `cargo fmt -p shirabe-validate` in the same branch,
because reverting the files does not stop the next format run from finding them
again. It merged in `232172a`. Verified formatting-only (line rewrapping and
trailing commas), so nothing is at risk, but it is churn in the history and it
put a reviewer's attention on the wrong lines.

The trap is that the safe-looking action is the one that causes it. An author
who formats only their own files is fine; an author who runs the obvious
workspace-wide command silently adopts every pre-existing deviation in the
crate.

## Direction

Format the tree once, in a commit that does nothing else, then gate it.

The order matters: gating first would fail every PR until someone does the
sweep, and sweeping without gating leaves the same trap armed for the next
drift. The sweep commit should be reviewable as "no semantic change" —
comparing both sides with whitespace and commas removed is enough to
demonstrate that.

Whether clippy joins the gate is a separate decision with a much larger first
sweep; this issue is only about `cargo fmt --check`.

## Acceptance

- `cargo fmt --all --check` exits 0 on `main`.
- CI fails a PR that leaves it non-zero.
- The sweep is its own commit, and its diff is demonstrably formatting-only.

## Not in scope

- `cargo clippy`.
- Changing the rustfmt configuration. This is about conforming to what the
  toolchain already produces, not about choosing a different style.

## fix(execute): preflight.sh aborts when CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT is unset

## Goal

Make `/execute`'s Step-1 preflight resolve the plugin root itself so it doesn't abort when `CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT` is not exported into the shell.

## Context

`skills/execute/scripts/preflight.sh:14` does:

```bash
ROOT="${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT:?CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT is not set; /execute cannot resolve the cross-skill child template}"
```

When the preflight is driven from a plain shell (for example, an agent running it through a Bash tool rather than the Claude-managed environment), `CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT` is not exported, so the script exits 1 before doing anything:

```
CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT is not set; /execute cannot resolve the cross-skill child template
```

This is the load-bearing cross-skill preflight (it asserts `work-on.md` resolves), so a hard failure here blocks the entire single-pr `/execute` run. The script lives at a fixed, known location inside the plugin (`skills/execute/scripts/`), so it can resolve the root from its own path instead of depending on an env var that the caller may not have set.

Observed on the released 0.12.0 plugin; the file is byte-identical on `main`, so it is unchanged.

## Reproduction

```bash
unset CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT
bash skills/execute/scripts/preflight.sh
# -> exit 1: "CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT is not set; /execute cannot resolve the cross-skill child template"
```

## Fix direction

Self-resolve the plugin root from the script's own path, falling back to the env var only when set, and keep the child-template existence check as the real assertion:

```bash
ROOT="${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT:-$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../../.." && pwd)}"
```

(`preflight.sh` is at `skills/execute/scripts/`, so `../../..` is the plugin root.)

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] `bash skills/execute/scripts/preflight.sh` succeeds when `CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT` is unset, provided the script is in its canonical location.
- [ ] When `CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT` is set, it still takes precedence (or both resolve to the same path).
- [ ] The cross-skill child-template check (`work-on.md`) remains the real assertion and still fails loudly when the template is missing.

## Unconditional fallback transitions fire on forwarded evidence, silently skipping required states

## Summary

When a state with a required `accepts` field is reached via an `advanced: true`
chain, koto's unconditional fallback transition fires using the forwarded evidence
from the *previous* state — skipping the current state's directive entirely.

## Steps to Reproduce

Given a template:

```yaml
states:
  A:
    accepts:
      status: {type: enum, values: [done], required: true}
    transitions:
      - target: B
        when: {status: done}

  B:
    accepts:
      result: {type: enum, values: [ok, fail], required: true}
    transitions:
      - target: C
        when: {result: ok}
      - target: D  # unconditional fallback — no when clause
```

1. Submit `{status: done}` to state A → transitions to B.
2. The forwarded `{status: done}` evidence does not match the `result: ok` transition in B.
3. koto fires the unconditional fallback `- target: D`, bypassing state B entirely.
4. `koto next` returns `action: done` / the D state without ever presenting B's directive.

## Observed Behavior

In the `work-on-plan.md` orchestrator template, submitting `finalization_status: updated`
to `pr_finalization` caused the workflow to chain through `ci_monitor` →
`plan_completion` → `done` in a single `koto next` call. Neither the CI verification
step nor the cascade script ran. The full response was:

```json
{"action":"done","advanced":true,"state":"done"}
```

Both `ci_monitor` and `plan_completion` have unconditional fallback transitions that
were triggered by the forwarded `finalization_status: updated` evidence.

## Expected Behavior

An unconditional fallback transition should only fire when the *current state's own*
evidence is submitted and doesn't match any conditional transition. It should not
fire because of evidence forwarded from a parent state.

Alternatively: states with `required: true` accepts fields should block advancement
entirely until matching evidence is submitted — even when reached via `advanced: true`.

## Impact

This can silently bypass states that perform required work (CI checks, cascades,
cleanup scripts). The behavior is especially dangerous in orchestrator templates
where each state has side effects.

## Workaround

Remove unconditional fallback transitions from states that must not be skipped.

## template export: send compilation warnings to stderr, not stdout

`koto template export template.md` writes compilation warnings (W3,
W4, etc.) to stdout, not stderr. When the command is redirected to a
file, the warnings pollute the output.

## Repro

```bash
$ koto template export skills/work-on/koto-templates/work-on.md > out.mermaid.md
$ head -3 out.mermaid.md
warning: W3: state "skipped_due_to_dep_failure": terminal state name suggests a failure outcome but `failure: true` is not set
  remedy: set `failure: true` if this state represents a failure, or rename it if it represents a success
stateDiagram-v2
```

The two-line warning is now part of the file.

## Expected

Warnings go to stderr so `koto template export > file` produces clean
output. Redirecting stderr separately (`2>warnings.log`) or
suppressing (`2>/dev/null`) then becomes explicit.

## Workaround

`2>/dev/null` (suppresses) or `2>warnings.log` (captures). Both are
easy but it's a footgun for first-time users and CI pipelines that
diff the output against a committed file.

## Suggestion

Route W\* warnings to stderr for all `koto template` subcommands. This
matches the convention of other CLI tools (e.g., rustc, clang) where
the artifact goes to stdout and diagnostics go to stderr.

## Seen in

Regenerating \`skills/work-on/koto-templates/work-on.mermaid.md\` in
tsukumogami/shirabe#78.

## fix(recipe): verify downloads against the published checksums.txt

Every koto release has published a checksums.txt alongside the binaries since the release workflow gained its "Generate checksums" step -- `sha256sum koto-* > checksums.txt`, uploaded in the workflow's explicit asset list -- but the recipe never pointed at it. The github_file action it used accepts no checksum parameter at all, so tsuku fell back to hashing whatever the release served at plan-generation time. That is enough to detect later corruption of a cached artifact, but there is nothing upstream to compare the first fetch against, so tsuku classified the download as unverified and said so on every install: "Note: 'koto' publishes no checksums", which was false.

Re-author the recipe as download + chmod + install_binaries so the download step can carry checksum_url, matching the shape shirabe's recipe already uses. The version source moves into an explicit [version] block with tag_prefix, since github_file's repo param was what inferred it before. The asset names and the resolved URL are unchanged.

This is a workaround for a gap in the action, not the end state. tsukumogami/tsuku#2537 tracks forwarding checksum_url and checksum_asset on github_file; once that ships this recipe goes back to the compact form plus a single checksum_asset line. The recipe carries a comment saying so.

---

## Why this surfaced

`tsuku update koto` printed a note on every run that `tsuku update shirabe` did not:

```
$ tsuku update koto
Note: Checksums for 'koto' will be computed during installation.
$ tsuku update shirabe
$
```

The note was accurate about what tsuku was doing and wrong about koto: we do publish checksums, the recipe just ignored them. (The note also printed on runs where nothing was installed at all, which is a separate tsuku bug fixed in tsukumogami/tsuku#2536.)

## Verification

```
$ tsuku validate .tsuku-recipes/koto.toml --strict
Valid recipe: koto
  Actions: download, chmod, install_binaries
  Binaries: bin/koto
  Verification: koto version
```

`Recipe.GetChecksumVerification()` now reports the recipe as statically verified rather than dynamic, which is what silences the note and puts koto in the same state as shirabe:

```
koto (before)   Dynamic (note prints)
koto (after)    Static (silent)
shirabe         Static (silent)
```

The asset names are unchanged (`koto-{os}-{arch}` across the four published targets), and the `v{version}` tag matches what previous plans resolved to -- a cached plan for koto 0.12.2 fetched `.../releases/download/v0.12.2/koto-linux-amd64`, byte-for-byte the URL this recipe builds. The Distributed Install (tsuku) check exercises the real fetch-and-verify path against a real release, so a mismatch between the manifest lines and the asset names would fail there rather than reaching users.

## Review notes

Worth a second opinion on one consequence: an install now fails loudly if `checksums.txt` is ever missing from a release, which is the point, but it does make that asset load-bearing. It is already in the workflow's explicit `ASSETS` array, so nothing further is needed to keep it there -- but a future edit to that array would break installs rather than silently downgrade verification.

The manual chain is more verbose than `github_file` for no benefit other than reaching the checksum field, which is exactly the escape hatch DESIGN-composite-action-checksum-support set out to eliminate. Reverting it is the first follow-up listed on tsukumogami/tsuku#2537.

## A durable DESIGN was deleted, stranding three upstream references

Three documents in this repository carry `upstream:` references to a DESIGN that was
deleted. DESIGN is a **durable** artifact — it should have moved to
`docs/designs/current/`, not been removed — so this is a different fault from
ephemeral-document references (#272) and is not covered by that issue's rule.

## The dangling references

```
[R6] upstream "docs/designs/DESIGN-roadmap-plan-standardization.md" does not exist on disk
  — docs/briefs/BRIEF-legend-vs-classdef-reconciliation.md:22
  — docs/briefs/BRIEF-lifecycle-passing-state-validation.md:18
  — docs/briefs/BRIEF-table-diagram-reconciliation.md:20
```

The target was removed in `a133581` ("chore(plan): verify-then-delete
roadmap-plan-standardization"), which deleted both a DESIGN and a PLAN in one commit. The
PLAN deletion is correct — plans are ephemeral and the cascade deletes them. The DESIGN
deletion is not: a design's terminal state is `Current` in `docs/designs/current/`, and it
stays on disk as the audit trail for how the implementation was chosen.

## Two questions this raises

1. **Why was a durable artifact deleted?** Either the cascade has a path that deletes a
   DESIGN rather than moving it, or this was a manual removal. Worth establishing which,
   because the first is a bug with recurrence risk and the second is not.
2. **What should happen to the three references now?** Restoring the DESIGN from history,
   re-pointing the briefs at a surviving ancestor, or dropping the field are all different
   answers with different audit-trail consequences.

## Why neither gate caught it

CI validates only the files a pull request changed, so an untouched sibling is never
checked. The whole-tree lifecycle check passes these three because they sit at a terminal
status, where the orphan rule permits them. They surface only in an explicit
whole-corpus per-file run.

## Related

- #272 — durable documents naming *ephemeral* ones as upstream. Same symptom class
  (dangling references), different cause. The other two of the five dangling references in
  this repository belong to that issue.

## feat(validate): add chain-aware passing-state lifecycle validation

## Goal

Add a `shirabe validate --lifecycle <root>` mode that walks the doc tree, identifies artifact chains (BRIEF ↔ PRD ↔ DESIGN ↔ PLAN/ROADMAP) via `upstream:` fields, infers each chain's posture from the PLAN's `execution_mode` and `status`, and verifies every doc in every chain is at its **passing state** — the state correct for the chain's current posture in this PR.

## Concepts

- **Target state**: the final sunny-path state a doc reaches. Fixed per artifact type — BRIEF Done, PRD Done, DESIGN Current, PLAN DELETED, ROADMAP DELETED.
- **Passing state**: the state a doc must be in for the PR currently under review to merge, for CI to be green, and for `--lifecycle` to exit success. Not fixed; depends on the chain's posture (single-pr vs multi-pr, in-flight vs work-completing). For a multi-pr chain in flight, BRIEF/PRD passing = Accepted (because the PLAN is at Active). For a work-completing PR (the PR where the multi-pr PLAN transitions Active → Done → DELETED), BRIEF/PRD passing = their target Done state. For a single-pr chain, BRIEF/PRD passing = their target Done state because the entire chain ships in one PR.

## Context

The existing diff-scoped validator can't see presence-without-touch. The previous PRD R17 codified two stateless L01/L02 checks — those are degenerate subsets of the passing-state concept and don't capture the chain-aware discipline the workspace actually needs. PR #167 (FC09) and PR #169 (FC08) both shipped single-pr chains where the BRIEF and PRD stopped at Accepted instead of transitioning to Done — drift the lifecycle gate as described here would have caught.

The `--lifecycle` mode walks the chain, not just the tree: from each PLAN/ROADMAP it reaches the BRIEF/PRD/DESIGN via inverse `upstream:` traversal, computes posture, and validates each chain member is at its passing state.

Design: extend `docs/designs/DESIGN-roadmap-plan-standardization.md` Decision 4 (and amend parent PRD R17/R18) in the chain landing this issue.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] `shirabe validate --lifecycle <root>` walks the doc tree, identifies artifact chains via `upstream:` traversal, and computes the passing state per chain posture (single-pr vs multi-pr; in-flight vs work-completing for multi-pr).
- [ ] The mode fails non-zero if any doc in any chain isn't at its passing state, naming the offending file, its current state, and its expected passing state.
- [ ] L01 (a multi-pr PLAN/ROADMAP at non-Active in the tree) and L02 (a single-pr PLAN present in the tree at merge time) are subsumed as degenerate cases of "doc isn't at passing state for this chain's posture."
- [ ] BRIEF/PRD/DESIGN passing-state validation: walks the chain from each PLAN/ROADMAP and verifies BRIEF/PRD are at the correct state given the chain's posture.
- [ ] The **orphan-doc question** (a BRIEF or PRD or DESIGN with no downstream PLAN/ROADMAP) is settled via a `/shirabe:decision` invocation during this issue's tactical chain. The decision outcome is encoded in the BRIEF's CUJs and enforced by the check.
- [ ] **Corpus reconciliation in this PR**: FC09 (PR #167) and FC08 (PR #169) shipped single-pr chains without driving their BRIEF and PRD to Done. The corpus is reconciled here: `docs/briefs/BRIEF-doc-vs-github-state-reconciliation.md` Accepted → Done; `docs/prds/PRD-doc-vs-github-state-reconciliation.md` Accepted → Done; `docs/briefs/BRIEF-legend-vs-classdef-reconciliation.md` Accepted → Done; `docs/prds/PRD-legend-vs-classdef-reconciliation.md` Accepted → Done. FC07 (PR #149) appears to have done this correctly; verify in this PR.
- [ ] **Parent PRD amendment**: `docs/prds/PRD-roadmap-plan-standardization.md` R17 and R18 are amended in this PR to codify the chain-aware passing-state model (replacing the two-stateless-checks framing). The check-code family choice (`Lnn` for lifecycle, distinct from `FCnn` for content) stays.
- [ ] Check codes use the `Lnn` family.
- [ ] SECURITY: walk bounded to the given doc-tree root, no symlink escape, defensive parsing of frontmatter (no panics on malformed `upstream:` cycles, missing fields, etc.).

## docs: design and plan for shirabe-cli-rust-rewrite

Adds two artifacts that decompose the shirabe `validate` CLI rewrite from Go to Rust: the accepted-then-planned technical design and the active implementation plan tracked through five GitHub issues.

`docs/designs/DESIGN-shirabe-cli-rust-rewrite.md` (status `Planned`) is the technical design for translating shirabe's `validate` CLI (~1,417 LOC of Go across `cmd/shirabe/` + `internal/validate/` + `internal/annotation/`) to Rust while preserving the public output contract byte-for-byte. Aligning shirabe's deterministic surface with koto's Rust substrate keeps cross-component composition structurally cheap and removes the Go/Rust seam that currently sits between shirabe and the rest of the toolkit's workflow tier.

The design locks seven decisions:

1. **YAML parser**: `saphyr` (the actively-maintained successor to `yaml-rust2`) with per-key `MarkedYamlOwned` line markers replacing `yaml.v3`'s `Node.Line`. Backstop documented to drop to `saphyr-parser`'s `SpannedEventReceiver` if the 0.0.x API drifts. Per-key line numbers are needed only for FC02 (`status` enum) and R6 (Plan `upstream` resolution) — FC03 and R7 read body section lines from a separate Markdown scan; SCHEMA/FC01/FC04 hardcode `line=1`.
2. **CLI framework**: `clap` v4 with `derive` macros, one struct per subcommand. Mechanical cobra → clap mapping documented so future subcommands inherit the idiom.
3. **Output-contract preservation**: a two-layer parity mechanism. Layer 1 — `tests/fixtures/golden/` in this repo: shirabe's own committed artifacts plus a synthetic edge-case corpus (FC02-trigger, R6-trigger, sanitize cases, parser stress-test inputs) asserted byte-equal against captured `shirabe-go-v0.6.1` output. Layer 2 — `.github/workflows/parity-check.yml`, a reusable workflow downstream callers include from their own CI to run the same parity assertion against their own corpora.
4. **Crate layout**: a Cargo workspace with `crates/shirabe-validate` (library, internal-shaped — exports may rename freely without semver until a downstream consumer commits) and `crates/shirabe` (binary). The workspace anticipates the library-crate boundary that follows from convergence with koto; workspace-from-day-one avoids restructuring every import path later.
5. **Tripwire-metrics subcommand timing**: ships as a follow-on PR. The metrics subcommand has no validation contract to preserve and shouldn't split the parity-fixture review attention.
6. **Rust toolchain pinning**: a specific stable version via `rust-toolchain.toml`. Deterministic builds; no nightly.
7. **Captured Go baseline pinning**: `v0.6.1` (the most recent tagged release) is the immutable parity baseline, capture script committed for reproducibility.

`docs/plans/PLAN-shirabe-cli-rust-rewrite.md` (status `Active`, mode multi-pr, milestone #7) decomposes the rewrite into five outline-shaped work units corresponding to the design's Implementation Approach phases. Multi-pr mode here means issue-tracked, not separately-merged: the issues exist so progress is visible and reviewable at the outline granularity, but all five close together when one cohesive replacement PR ships per the design's `no-Go-Rust-feature-flag-coexistence` commitment.

| Outline | Issue | Complexity |
|---------|-------|------------|
| O1: Cargo workspace skeleton | [#129](https://github.com/tsukumogami/shirabe/issues/129) | simple |
| O2: Frontmatter parser and Doc/FormatSpec types | [#130](https://github.com/tsukumogami/shirabe/issues/130) | testable |
| O3: Validation checks and annotation emitter | [#131](https://github.com/tsukumogami/shirabe/issues/131) | critical |
| O4: Binary crate and CLI surface | [#132](https://github.com/tsukumogami/shirabe/issues/132) | testable |
| O5: Golden-output fixture, parity workflow, and release pipeline cut | [#133](https://github.com/tsukumogami/shirabe/issues/133) | critical |

The dependency chain is strictly linear (O1 → O2 → O3 → O4 → O5); the eventual rewrite PR's suggested commit structure is documented in the PLAN's Implementation Sequence section. Total estimated effort: roughly one engineer-week of focused work.

---

## Substantive design properties worth reviewer attention

- **Two-layer parity preservation.** The reusable `parity-check.yml` workflow lets downstream callers — including future external adopters this repo doesn't know about — assert the same byte equality against their own corpora without embedding their artifacts into this repo. The Decision 3 "Why two layers" subsection names both the constraint (visibility separation across caller boundaries) and the generalization (preservation contract extends to arbitrary callers).
- **YAML risk distribution, not concentration.** The rewrite's single non-trivial risk surface is the per-key line-number reconstruction. Picking `saphyr` distributes that risk across an actively-maintained parser with built-in `Span` markers, instead of concentrating it in a hand-rolled scanner over `serde_yaml`'s position-erasing output. The Go side carried no equivalent fragility (yaml.v3 has native `Node.Line`); the design preserves that property.
- **Workspace-from-day-one asymmetry.** Cost now: one `Cargo.toml` split. Cost of single-crate-now-restructure-later: renaming every import path that crosses the new crate boundary at exactly the moment the library-API publication design is negotiating stability. The asymmetry favors workspace from day one; the three-crate alternative is rejected as actual YAGNI.
- **Hand-written `impl std::error::Error` over thiserror.** The error surface is small (two variants, structured fields); thiserror buys nothing and would leak through the future-published crate boundary as a public dependency on a derive macro.
- **Extending-the-validator convention** is documented in §Solution Architecture so future contributors don't grep the design to add a new check or format: a check is `fn check_<name>(&Doc, &FormatSpec, &Config) -> Vec<ValidationError>` called from `validate_file`; a new format is one entry in `FORMATS` plus optionally a `match` arm.

## docs: design installation and distribution

## Goal

Write `docs/designs/DESIGN-koto-installation.md` specifying how koto is released,
how users install it, and what the first-run experience looks like.

## Context

koto is a Go CLI binary with no runtime dependencies. Getting koto working
end-to-end requires three steps:

1. **Binary on the machine** -- the user installs koto
2. **Integration into the project** -- something puts koto-aware configuration into the project so agents discover and use koto
3. **Agent invokes koto** -- the agent calls koto CLI commands during workflow execution

This design covers **step 1 only**. Step 3 is the engine (already built). Step 2
is unsolved and covered by a separate design.

The template search path must not include world-writable or shared directories by
default (security constraint from the template format design).

## Scope

The design should cover:

- **Release automation**: GoReleaser configuration (platforms, checksums), GitHub
  Release asset structure, CI workflow
- **Self-contained install script**: a curl-pipe-sh installer (like tsuku and Claude
  Code have) that downloads the right binary for the platform, verifies it, and puts
  it on PATH. This is koto's own installation channel and opens the door for
  auto-update in the future.
- **tsuku recipe**: TOML recipe following tsuku conventions, GitHub releases version
  provider, checksum verification, install to ~/.tsuku/bin/. Eating our own dogfood.
- **Template search path**: ordered directory list with security justification, override
  mechanism
- **Built-in template distribution**: go:embed vs filesystem loading trade-offs
- **First-run experience**: what a user sees after install, and guidance toward project
  integration (step 2, whatever form that takes)
- **Version reporting**: koto version output (version, commit SHA, build date via
  GoReleaser ldflags)

## Deferred

- **Third-party package managers** (Homebrew, apt, Scoop, etc.) -- deferred until the
  tool is stable. GoReleaser already produces the binaries they'd need, so adding
  channels later is straightforward.
- **Agent integration** -- how agents discover koto in a project (separate design)
- **Template format specification** -- already shipped

## Out of Scope

- Human-facing slash command UX -- separate design
- go install as a primary channel (works by default for Go users, no design needed)
